root_causes.description: Article list serializer issues per-article queries and page size is caller-controlled without a cap.
Comments list is unbounded and not preloaded.
AR connection pool not sized to Puma thread count.
Single-file SQLite as production datastore with default journal mode.
List ordering column unindexed; full count per request.
Tag popularity recomputed per request instead of read from maintained counter.

findings.problem: Article list and feed serialize each article with per-row queries (favorited?, following? on the author, tag_list without preloaded tags) while the page size comes from params[:limit] with no server-side maximum, so per-request query count is caller-controlled.
findings.performance_principle: Per-item work in a list must be batched, and the size of a list a caller can request must be bounded by the server.

evidence.statement: Same uncapped limit on the feed action
:tag_list serialized per article without includes(:tags); per-row load inferred from acts-as-taggable-on 3.5.0 API, not verified in repo
Derivation: queries per signed-in list request = 3 fixed (count, page, user preload) + 3 per article = 3 + 3N; 63 at N=20, 3003 at limit=1000. Anonymous: 3 + N.
No runtime evidence exists (no query log, trace, or profile supplied).

findings.conditions: Matters at default N=20 under moderate traffic (63 queries per signed-in page) and becomes an outage mechanism when any caller sends a large limit; assumption: such requests occur or can be sent, since the endpoint is unauthenticated. Workload unknown, so confidence capped at Medium.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched controller, before_actions, middleware and routes for a limit clamp; none found.
Searched for includes/preload/eager_load of tags or favorites and memoization of favorited?/following?; none found.
favorites_count is counter-cached, so the favorites count is not N+1; only favorited? is.
Whether tag_list queries per row depends on gem internals not present in the repo.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If clients only ever send the default 20 and traffic is low, 63 indexed point queries against an in-process SQLite file may cost only a few milliseconds in total.
findings.recommendation: Clamp limit (and offset) server-side to a team-chosen maximum; preload tags and fetch the viewer's favorited article ids and followed author ids for the page in one query each, passing them to the partial as sets, so query count is constant in page size.

alternatives.option: Clamp limit and batch-load favorites/follows/tags per page
alternatives.why: Removes and bounds the work with no new infrastructure or staleness.
Stops the unbounded case but leaves 3N queries per page.
Per-viewer fields force per-user keys with poor hit rate and invalidation on every favorite/follow; hides work.

findings.trade_offs: A cap changes API behaviour for clients relying on large pages; batching adds controller code and two constant extra queries; preloading tags fetches tag rows clients may ignore.

validation.metric: SQL statements per GET /api/articles request at limit=20 vs limit=100 (signed in)
validation.expectation: Before: count grows by about 3 per added article (derived 3 + 3N). After: constant independent of limit. Latency change unquantified until measured.
validation.falsifier: Query count already constant across limit values.
validation.guard: Integration test asserting identical query count for 5 and 20 articles via sql.active_record subscription, plus a test that limit=10000 returns at most the cap.

commands.purpose: Generate the per-request SQL log in log/development.log to count queries per article.

findings.problem: Comments index returns every comment for an article with no limit and no includes(:user); the partial loads each author and, when signed in, runs following? per comment.
findings.performance_principle: Per-item lookups in a list must be batched, and list responses must be bounded.

evidence.statement: @article.comments.order(created_at: :desc) with no includes and no limit
Derivation: 2 fixed (article lookup, comment list) + 2 per comment = 2 + 2C, C uncapped.

findings.conditions: Matters for articles with many comments; largest comment count per article is unknown. C grows with per-article activity, not total table size.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for pagination or a default scope on Comment; none found.
comments.article_id is indexed, so the outer query is cheap; only per-row lookups and payload size matter.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Most articles receive a handful of comments; at about 5 comments this is roughly a dozen point queries.
findings.recommendation: Add includes(:user), batch the viewer's follow lookups for distinct author ids in one query, and add a server-side cap or pagination.

alternatives.option: Preload authors, batch follow lookup, and cap
alternatives.why: Removes per-item work and bounds the response.

findings.trade_offs: Pagination changes the RealWorld response contract; clients may need updating.

validation.metric: SQL statements per GET /api/articles/:slug/comments on an article seeded with 50 comments
validation.expectation: Constant query count independent of comment count after the change.
validation.falsifier: Query count already constant in comment count.

findings.problem: ActiveRecord pool is 5 per process while Puma 3.4 runs with no configuration, i.e. its default of up to 16 threads; above 5 concurrent DB-bound requests, threads queue for connections and fail after the 5 s checkout timeout.
findings.performance_principle: Pool size must match the number of concurrent workers that need it, or queueing for the pool becomes the dominant hidden latency.

evidence.statement: No config/puma.rb, Procfile, Dockerfile, or start script in the repository (full file listing).
Derivation: Puma 3.x documented default max threads 16 minus pool 5 = 11 threads per process that can wait for a connection at full concurrency.

findings.conditions: Assumes production starts Puma with defaults (no config in repo) and sees bursts above 5 concurrent DB-bound requests per process.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for config/puma.rb, Procfile, bin scripts, RAILS_MAX_THREADS-driven pool, Dockerfiles; none found.
Actual production start command is unknown.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: At 5 or fewer concurrent in-flight requests per process the pool is never exhausted, and under the GVL extra threads add limited CPU parallelism anyway.
findings.recommendation: Add config/puma.rb with explicit threads/workers and drive both Puma threads and the AR pool from one env var so they cannot diverge; keep thread count modest on SQLite.

alternatives.option: Puma threads = AR pool from a single env var
alternatives.why: Removes the mismatch at its source; standard Rails practice.
On SQLite extra connections add no write concurrency and increase SQLITE_BUSY contention.
Works but without a single source of truth.

findings.trade_offs: Fewer threads lowers per-process I/O concurrency; more processes cost memory.

validation.metric: Puma busy threads/backlog and count of ActiveRecord::ConnectionTimeoutError in production logs
validation.expectation: No connection checkout timeouts at the same concurrency after aligning threads and pool.
validation.falsifier: Production already runs with 5 or fewer threads per process.
validation.guard: Boot-time assertion that connection pool size >= Puma max threads.

findings.problem: Production uses a single SQLite file with no journal_mode configured: every write serializes on the file lock, rollback-journal commits block readers, contended requests wait up to the 5000 ms busy timeout, and the file is host-local.
findings.performance_principle: A single serialization point shared by all writes caps write throughput regardless of added workers.

evidence.statement: No PRAGMA journal_mode anywhere in config/, db/, or initializers.
counter_cache: true makes each favorite two writes

findings.conditions: Matters only if production actually runs on SQLite and sees concurrent writes or needs more than one host; both unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for DATABASE_URL override, pg/mysql2 gems, or platform config; Gemfile declares only sqlite3.
This is the RealWorld example app; SQLite in production may not reflect a real deployment.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: For a single-host, low-write blog workload SQLite (especially with WAL) is adequate and its in-process reads are fast.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the production engine first; if SQLite stays, enable WAL and keep threads equal to pool; migrate to a client-server engine only on multi-host or write-concurrency evidence.

alternatives.why: Cheapest change removing reader/writer blocking with no new infrastructure.
Removes single-writer and single-host limits at real operational cost; needs evidence.

findings.trade_offs: WAL adds -wal/-shm files and checkpoint management; engine migration is a substantial operational change.

validation.metric: PRAGMA journal_mode result and count of 'database is locked' / SQLite3::BusyException in production logs
validation.expectation: After WAL, readers no longer wait on commits; busy errors fall.
validation.falsifier: Production already runs another engine or WAL is already enabled.

findings.problem: Every article list request runs a full COUNT and an ORDER BY created_at with OFFSET/LIMIT on a table with no created_at index, so the unfiltered list scans and sorts the whole articles table.
findings.performance_principle: A per-request query returning a fixed-size page should not cost proportional to total table size.

evidence.statement: articles indexes only on slug and user_id
No query plan examined; no runtime evidence exists.

findings.conditions: Matters once articles grows to a size where a full scan is noticeable; row count unknown. Filtered variants are narrowed first by indexed joins.

counter_evidence.statement: Checked all migrations and schema.rb for a created_at index; none.
SQLite uses a bounded top-N sorter with LIMIT, so memory is bounded though the scan is not.
articlesCount is part of the API contract, so the count cannot simply be removed.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: A small site may never accumulate enough articles for a local-file scan to register.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN; if it shows a temp B-tree sort, add an index on articles(created_at); decide explicitly whether an exact total is required on every page.

alternatives.option: Index created_at after confirming the plan
alternatives.why: Makes the page query proportional to offset+limit at small write cost.
Also removes OFFSET cost but changes the public API contract.
Invalidated by every new article; hides the scan.

findings.trade_offs: Index adds insert cost and storage; building it takes the SQLite write lock for its duration.

validation.metric: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output for the article list query
validation.expectation: After indexing, plan uses the created_at index with no USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY.
validation.falsifier: Current plan already avoids the temp B-tree, or the table is small enough that timings are flat.
validation.guard: CI check running EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on this query and failing on a temp B-tree sort.

commands.command: sqlite3 db/production.sqlite3 "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT articles.* FROM articles ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0;"
commands.purpose: Show whether the list query scans and sorts with a temp B-tree.

findings.problem: GET /api/tags computes Article.tag_counts.most_used, a grouped aggregate over all Article taggings, on every unauthenticated request to return 20 names, although tags.taggings_count is already maintained.
findings.performance_principle: Do not recompute per read an aggregate that is already maintained incrementally on write.

evidence.statement: GROUP BY over taggings is inferred from acts-as-taggable-on 3.5.0's API; not visible in the repo.

findings.conditions: Assumes /api/tags is requested about as often as the home page and taggings grows into the thousands or more; both unverified.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for Rails.cache, HTTP caching, fresh_when around the endpoint; none.
most_used caps the result at 20 rows but not the scan.
Gem-generated SQL not verifiable from the repo.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: taggings may stay small; and taggings_count counts all taggable types, which is a legitimate reason to prefer the scoped query if other models are ever tagged.
findings.recommendation: Read top tags from ActsAsTaggableOn::Tag.most_used(20) ordered by taggings_count (only Article is taggable here), after confirming the current SQL in a query log.

alternatives.why: Removes the work; data already maintained on write.
Keeps the expensive query on every miss and needs a cache store that is not configured.

findings.trade_offs: Counts would include any future non-Article taggings; counter can drift if taggings are written outside the gem.

validation.metric: SQL issued by GET /api/tags and its EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
validation.expectation: Replacement is a single ORDER BY taggings_count LIMIT 20 on tags with no GROUP BY over taggings.
validation.falsifier: Current SQL already avoids a GROUP BY over taggings.

findings.problem: Production log level is :debug, so every SQL statement is formatted and written synchronously on the request thread, amplified by PERF-001's per-article queries.
findings.performance_principle: Instrumentation overhead must be proportionate; per-operation logging on a hot path multiplies with its amplification.

evidence.statement: No RAILS_LOG_LEVEL override or custom logger found.

findings.conditions: Holds at any traffic; magnitude scales with queries per request and request rate.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for log level env override or custom logger; none.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Buffered file logging is cheap per line, and fixing PERF-001 cuts the line count.
findings.recommendation: Set production log level to :info and use sampled or on-demand debug logging for investigation.

alternatives.why: Removes per-query log writes with a one-line change.
Costly, unstructured substitute for real instrumentation.

findings.trade_offs: Removes the only current per-query visibility in production; pair with PERF-008.

validation.metric: Log bytes and SQL lines per request in production logs
validation.expectation: SQL lines disappear from production logs.
validation.falsifier: Production already overrides the log level at deploy time.

findings.problem: No APM, metrics, per-request query count, or pool wait-time instrumentation exists, so no performance finding can be confirmed or a fix validated in production.
findings.performance_principle: A system must be measured before it is optimized.

evidence.statement: No APM, metrics, or profiler gems declared

findings.conditions: Applies at any workload; prerequisite for validating every other finding.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched initializers, Gemfile, lib/ for instrumentation; none found.

findings.recommendation: Add per-request duration and SQL query count (sql.active_record subscriber or APM agent) and Puma thread/backlog stats, sequenced before or alongside PERF-001.
findings.trade_offs: Small per-request overhead and a new dependency or agent.

validation.metric: Per-endpoint query count and p95 duration visible in metrics
validation.expectation: Metrics exist for every route after the change.
validation.falsifier: Not applicable beyond a presence check; if metrics already exist elsewhere, the finding is void.

considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Likely dominated by PERF-001 I/O; no profile shows CPU is a meaningful share.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: A stackprof profile shows template rendering as a top frame after PERF-001 is fixed.

considered_not_reported.observation: bcrypt cost 11 on login and registration
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Intentional security cost, bounded per login, low frequency.

considered_not_reported.observation: dependent: :destroy cascades instantiate each child on article/user delete
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Rare operation bounded by per-article children; path currently broken (COR-001).
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Bulk deletes or very large comment threads appear.

considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Uses user_id and fk_follows indexes; bounded by followed authors; shares already-reported PERF-001/PERF-005 costs.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: A user follows thousands of authors.

considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Single HMAC verification; constant and negligible next to DB work.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: A profile shows auth as a top frame.

adjacent_findings.problem: Article declares has_many :articles, dependent: :destroy; articles has no article_id column, so destroying an article should raise a SQL error and roll back, breaking DELETE /api/articles/:slug.

evidence.statement: articles table has no article_id column

adjacent_findings.recommendation: Remove the association and add a destroy-path test.
adjacent_findings.assessed_properly_by: A correctness-focused test suite covering destroy paths.

adjacent_findings.problem: favorites.find_or_create_by is check-then-insert with no unique (user_id, article_id) index; concurrent requests can create duplicates and inflate favorites_count.

evidence.statement: only single-column non-unique indexes on favorites

adjacent_findings.recommendation: Add a unique composite index on favorites(user_id, article_id) and rescue RecordNotUnique.
adjacent_findings.assessed_properly_by: A data-integrity review with concurrency tests.

evidence.statement: locked versions of rails, devise, jwt, puma
